title: Death Toll Rises to 40 After Russian Strike on Ukrainian Aid Site, Dozens Still Missing
body:
The death toll from a Russian airstrike on an aid distribution centre in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region has climbed to 40, with dozens more still unaccounted for, officials said on Monday. The attack, which hit a humanitarian hub in the town of Vasylivka, underscores the growing danger that civilians and aid workers face as the war drags into its third year, and it has sparked fresh condemnation from Western governments and humanitarian organisations.

The strike hit the centre just after noon, when crowds of displaced residents had gathered to collect food, water and medical supplies that had been delivered by the United Nations and local NGOs. According to regional authorities, the explosion destroyed the makeshift warehouse and nearby tents, killing at least 40 people and injuring many more. Rescue teams from the State Emergency Service, along with volunteers from the Red Cross, have been searching the rubble for survivors; the number of missing persons is estimated at 30‑40, though officials warn that the figure could rise as more bodies are recovered.

International reaction has been swift. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) described the bombing as “a blatant violation of international humanitarian law” and called for an immediate investigation. European Union foreign ministers issued a joint statement demanding that Russia halt attacks on civilian infrastructure, while the United States warned of “additional sanctions” if the pattern of targeting aid sites continues. Humanitarian groups, including Médecins Sans Frontières and the International Committee of the Red Cross, have warned that such incidents jeopardise the delivery of life‑saving assistance to millions of Ukrainians already living in precarious conditions.

The Zaporizhzhia region, which lies along the front line between Russian‑occupied territories and Ukrainian‑controlled areas, has become a flashpoint for civilian casualties. Since the start of the invasion, the United Nations estimates that more than 7,000 civilians have been killed in the region, many of them in attacks on schools, hospitals and markets. Analysts say the recent strike may be part of a broader Russian strategy to disrupt supply lines and undermine the morale of communities that depend on external aid. “Targeting an aid depot sends a chilling message that no place is safe, even where humanitarian actors operate under the protection of international law,” said Dr. Elena Koval, a senior researcher at the Institute for Conflict Studies in Kyiv.

For the residents of Vasylivka, the tragedy is a stark reminder of the war’s relentless toll. Survivors described scenes of panic as the blast ripped through the courtyard, sending debris and shrapnel into the crowd. “We came here to get food for our children,” said Olena, a mother of three who managed to escape with minor injuries. “Now we are left with nothing but grief.” Local officials have declared a state of emergency and are coordinating with neighbouring towns to establish temporary shelters for those displaced by the attack.

Looking ahead, the humanitarian community faces a daunting challenge: how to continue delivering aid in an environment where even clearly marked distribution points are vulnerable to attack. Aid agencies are already considering alternative methods, such as aerial drops and mobile clinics, to reduce the risk to both recipients and staff. Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts to hold perpetrators accountable are intensifying, with the International Criminal Court reportedly gathering evidence of potential war crimes. As the death count rises and the list of missing grows, the incident at Vasylivka may become a pivotal moment in the international response to the conflict, shaping both the rules of engagement on the battlefield and the mechanisms for protecting civilians in war zones.
